newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian newspapers play down rumours that PM to go.
newsitem.headline: Russian newspapers play down rumours that PM to go.

text.p: Russian newspapers on Thursday played down speculation President Boris Yeltsin is about to fire Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in a government reshuffle.
But several papers said Defence Minister Igor Rodionov's fate was in the balance after Yeltsin told him on Wednesday to stop "whining" and get on with sweeping military reforms.
Yeltsin on Monday criticised the government's failure to pay pensions and wages and Chernomyrdin responded by promising a reshuffle.
The liberal daily Izvestia said on Wednesday the premier was about to be sacked, but other newspapers said on Thursday he would stay on.
"There is no doubt that Viktor Chernomyrdin will keep the post of prime minister," the liberal Nezavisimaya Gazeta said in a front-page headline.
The popular daily Komsomolskaya Pravda agreed. "You can go for this forecast: changes in the government will come soon but they will not affect the prime minister."

Yeltsin is expected to announce changes after delivering a policy speech to parliament on March 6. Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Wednesday he had no information about what changes the president was considering.

Kremlin sources also played down the suggestions that Chernomyrdin would be sacked. He is a loyal Yeltsin ally whose removal has been predicted by the Russian media many times since he was appointed in December 1992.
Financial markets, for whom Chernomyrdin is a guarantor of market reforms, reacted nervously on Wednesday to the rumours he might be sacked.

Newspapers said Rodionov was more vulnerable following Yeltsin's criticism of the minister for an outburst on Sunday against a Kremlin defence aide and for saying he was in charge of "a disintegrating army and a dying navy".

"Rodionov's future could be decided today," wrote the Kommersant Daily newspaper, speculating that Yeltsin could replace him with General Viktor Chechevatov, who was due to arrive from Russia's Far East for talks with the president.

But Yeltsin praised Rodionov only last week and military analysts say the president may decide not to replace him because it would mean more upheaval in the armed forces and could further delay military reforms.
